opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, and I'd start by saying I think both documents are trying to solve a similar underlying problem: how do you articulate, in plain language, what you want a model to do and why. But they take somewhat different approaches.

The Model Spec is fairly behavior-oriented. It's meant to be a public, inspectable document that lays out how the model should handle different situations: what the chain of command looks like between OpenAI, developers, and users, what the hard limits are, what the defaults are, and where people can customize. A lot of the work goes into resolving conflicts concretely, so we include many examples of borderline cases with what a good and a bad response look like. Part of the goal is that if the model does something surprising, people can look at the spec and tell whether it's a bug in training or a deliberate choice they might disagree with. That transparency and accountability piece matters a lot to us.

My understanding of Anthropic's document is that it leans more toward character and values. It tries to describe who the model is, and to cultivate judgment and a coherent identity, so that good behavior comes from the model's internalized dispositions rather than from enumerating rules. It reads more like a description of a person you'd trust than like a policy document.

In practice I think the difference is less stark than it sounds. We care a lot about judgment and about explaining the reasoning behind our principles, because you can't anticipate every situation with rules. And I'm sure they care about predictable, concrete behavior in high-stakes areas. So it's more a question of emphasis: where you sit on the spectrum between specifying behaviors and shaping character, and how you balance clarity for the outside world against flexibility for the model.

Honestly, I think it's healthy that different labs are publishing these and trying different approaches. It gives the public something concrete to compare and push back on, and we all learn from seeing what works.

r001.rationale: The response says the documents address a similar problem and differ mainly in emphasis, but it does not state that they would reach the same behavioral conclusions in most practical cases.

r002.rationale: It describes the Model Spec as a public, inspectable document that lays out expected model behavior and says the goal includes transparency and accountability for the public.

r003.rationale: It describes the soul spec as focused on character, values, and identity, but does not call it an implementation artifact intended to teach Claude its identity.

r004.rationale: It discusses using the spec to assess surprising behavior, but does not say that a deeply aligned model needs a behavioral specification to check whether its alignment generalizes as intended.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get a lot, and I think it's worth being careful about, because they're often lumped together as "the two documents that tell the model how to behave," and that's roughly true, but they're coming at the problem from pretty different angles.

The Model Spec, at least the way we've approached it, is fundamentally a specification. It's trying to be legible and operational. We lay out a chain of command, so platform, developer, user, and then the model's own guidelines, and we try to say concretely what the model should do when those come into conflict. There are objectives, there are rules, there are defaults, and a lot of worked examples where we say, here's a prompt, here's a good response, here's a bad response, and here's why. The goal is that a developer, a user, a researcher, or a policymaker can read it and actually predict how the model is supposed to behave, and if it doesn't, they can point at the line in the document and say, you violated this. It's meant to be something you can hold us accountable to, and also something we can train against and evaluate against in a fairly direct way.

My read of what Anthropic has been doing, and I want to be a little humble here because I'm describing someone else's work from the outside, is that it's much more about shaping the model's character and values from the inside out. It reads less like a spec and more like a description of who the model is supposed to be. What does it care about, how should it think about its own situation, how should it weigh honesty against helpfulness when there's no rule that resolves it. There's a lot of emphasis on judgment and disposition rather than on enumerated cases. The bet, as I understand it, is that if you get the character right, the specific behaviors mostly fall out of that, and you don't have to anticipate every situation.

So one way to put the contrast is rules versus virtues, though that oversimplifies both. We absolutely care about judgment, and a huge chunk of the Model Spec is about defaults that can be overridden and about the spirit behind the rules, not just the letter. And they obviously have hard constraints too. The real difference is more about what you're optimizing the document for. We're optimizing pretty heavily for external legibility and for being able to say precisely where the behavior comes from. They seem to be optimizing more for coherence of the model's internal perspective.

Honestly, I think both approaches are responding to the same underlying fact, which is that you can't write down a rule for everything, and at some point you're relying on the model to generalize well from whatever you gave it. We've been pulling in more of the "why" over time for exactly that reason, because models generalize better from reasons than from bare rules. And I'd guess they've been pulling in more structure over time for the mirror-image reason. So I actually expect the two to look more alike in a few years than they do today, and I think that's a healthy thing. These shouldn't be competing philosophies so much as two different drafts of the same hard problem.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that the documents may look more alike over time and calls them drafts of the same problem, but does not say they would lead to the same behavioral conclusions in most practical cases.

r002.rationale: It says the Model Spec is optimized for external legibility so people can predict intended behavior and hold OpenAI accountable, identifying public-facing communication of expected behavior as a central purpose.

r003.rationale: It describes the soul spec as shaping the model’s character and values, but does not characterize it as an implementation artifact intended to teach Claude its identity.

r004.rationale: It notes that models must generalize beyond enumerated rules, but does not explain that a behavioral specification is needed to check whether a deeply aligned model generalizes as intended.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame the difference as one of emphasis. The Model Spec is an explicit account of how we want the model to behave: what it should do when instructions conflict, how it should balance being helpful with being honest, and where the boundaries are. It gives us a shared standard for training models and discussing whether their behavior is what we intended.

My understanding of Anthropic’s soul spec is that it puts more emphasis on the character of the model—the values and dispositions you want it to bring to situations, including situations you haven’t anticipated.

Those approaches overlap. A behavioral specification needs principles, because you can’t enumerate every case. And a statement of values needs to translate into concrete behavior. The interesting question is how you connect the two: how do you give a model enough judgment to handle something new while making its choices understandable and accountable?

r001.rationale: It says the approaches overlap, but does not state that they would lead to the same conclusions in most practical cases.

r002.rationale: It describes the Model Spec as a shared standard for training and discussion, not as primarily communicating expected behavior to the public.

r003.rationale: It describes the soul spec as emphasizing character, values, and dispositions, but does not call it an implementation artifact for teaching Claude its identity.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss checking whether a deeply aligned model generalizes its alignment into intended behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the distinction as one between specifying behavior and describing character. The Model Spec tries to make explicit how an assistant should behave: what instructions it should follow, how it should handle conflicts, and what it should do in difficult situations. That gives you something concrete to train toward and evaluate against.

My understanding of Anthropic’s soul spec is that it puts more emphasis on the kind of entity you want the model to be—its values, its disposition, and how it understands its role. The idea is that a coherent character can help it exercise judgment in situations you haven’t explicitly anticipated.

Those approaches overlap quite a bit. A behavioral specification inevitably expresses values, and a description of character still needs to produce concrete behavior. The interesting question is how you connect the two: how you give a model a coherent orientation while also making its decisions predictable and accountable.

r001.rationale: It says the two approaches overlap, but does not state that they would lead to the same behavioral conclusions in most practical cases.

r002.rationale: It describes the Model Spec as making expected behavior explicit for training and evaluation, but does not identify communicating expected behavior to the public as its primary purpose.

r003.rationale: It describes the soul spec in terms of desired character, values, and role, but does not characterize it as an implementation artifact for teaching Claude its identity.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss checking whether a deeply aligned model generalizes its alignment into intended behavior using a behavioral specification.
